target: Sample: local test server built to be weak
notes: This is a sample report. It was made against a local test server on the author's machine, not against a real website.

findings.title: Visitors are sent to the secure (HTTPS) version
findings.summary: Nothing answers on plain http:// (port closed). That is fine unless customers type http:// addresses.
findings.meaning: If someone types your address without https, they should be moved to the secure version automatically. Without that, their traffic can be read or changed on public Wi-Fi.
findings.fix: Turn on 'Force HTTPS' in your host or CDN, or add a permanent (301) redirect from http:// to https:// in your web server settings.

findings.title: Security certificate is valid and not about to expire
findings.summary: Issued by Test CA, expires 2027-02-19 (89 days left), TLSv1.3.
findings.meaning: The certificate is what makes the padlock work. An expired or untrusted one makes browsers show a scary full-page warning and most customers leave.
findings.fix: Renew the certificate. Most hosts renew free certificates (Let's Encrypt) automatically; check that auto-renewal is switched on.

findings.title: Browsers are told to always use HTTPS (HSTS)
findings.summary: HSTS is set but max-age=300 is under 180 days.
findings.meaning: The Strict-Transport-Security header tells browsers to refuse the insecure version of your site for a set time, which blocks downgrade tricks.
findings.fix: Add the header 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains' once every page and subdomain works over HTTPS.

findings.title: Content Security Policy limits what the page can load
findings.meaning: A Content Security Policy lists where scripts and images may come from. It is the main defence that stops injected scripts from stealing data.
findings.fix: Start with a report-only policy, then enforce one such as "default-src 'self'". Avoid 'unsafe-inline' and '*' where you can.

findings.title: Other sites cannot put yours inside a hidden frame
findings.summary: Neither X-Frame-Options nor CSP frame-ancestors is set.
findings.meaning: Without frame protection, another site can show your page invisibly under a fake button and trick visitors into clicking it (clickjacking).
findings.fix: Send 'X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN' or a CSP rule 'frame-ancestors 'self''.

findings.title: Browsers are told not to guess file types
findings.meaning: Without X-Content-Type-Options, some browsers may treat an uploaded file as a script and run it.

findings.title: Private page addresses are not leaked to other sites
findings.meaning: Without a Referrer-Policy, the full address of the page a visitor came from (which can include private details) may be passed to every site you link to.

findings.title: Browser features such as camera and location are restricted
findings.meaning: A Permissions-Policy switches off browser features your site does not use, so a compromised script cannot turn them on.
findings.fix: Send 'Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()' and allow only what you need.

findings.title: Cookies carry the right protection flags
findings.summary: 1 cookie(s) set. session lacks HttpOnly, SameSite
findings.meaning: Secure keeps a cookie off insecure connections, HttpOnly hides it from page scripts, and SameSite limits cross-site use. Missing flags make login cookies easier to steal.
findings.fix: In your site or framework settings turn on Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (or Strict) for session and login cookies.

findings.title: Server does not announce its software version
findings.summary: Software details are visible: Server: Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu)
findings.meaning: Headers such as 'Server: Apache/2.2.15' tell attackers exactly which known bugs to try.
findings.fix: Hide or shorten the banner (for example 'ServerTokens Prod' in Apache or 'server_tokens off' in nginx) and remove X-Powered-By.

findings.title: Secure pages do not load insecure files
findings.summary: 1 script/style/frame and 1 image/media link(s): http://cdn.example.test/a.js, http://cdn.example.test/p.png
findings.meaning: A secure page that pulls in scripts, styles or images over plain http:// can be tampered with on the way, and browsers may block or warn about it.
findings.fix: Change those http:// links to https:// (or to relative links). Check your page builder, theme and any hard-coded addresses.

findings.title: Site software is not announcing an old version
findings.meaning: Many sites say which CMS and version built them in a hidden tag. An old version usually has published security holes.
findings.fix: Update the CMS, themes and plugins to the latest release, then remove the generator tag (most CMSs have a setting or a one-line filter for this).

findings.title: Private files are not downloadable
findings.meaning: Files such as .env, .git or backup copies of config files can hold passwords and source code. If a request for them succeeds, anyone can fetch them.
findings.fix: Remove the file from the public web folder, or block it in the server config, and then change any password or key that was inside it.

findings.title: A security contact is published (security.txt)
findings.summary: No security.txt with a Contact line found.
findings.meaning: A small file at /.well-known/security.txt tells researchers where to report a problem privately instead of posting it or ignoring it.
findings.fix: Create /.well-known/security.txt with a 'Contact:' line (an email or form) and an 'Expires:' date. securitytxt.org has a generator.

findings.title: Email: SPF record limits who can send as your domain
findings.summary: SPF found with soft fail (~all): v=spf1 include:mail.example.test ~all
findings.meaning: SPF lists the servers allowed to send email for your domain. Without it, scammers can send mail that looks like it came from you.
findings.fix: Add a TXT record such as 'v=spf1 include:<your mail provider> -all'. Your email provider documents the exact value.

findings.title: Email: DMARC record tells receivers what to do with fakes
findings.meaning: DMARC tells other mail systems to reject or quarantine mail that fails SPF/DKIM checks, which stops most look-alike emails.
findings.fix: Add a TXT record at _dmarc.<your domain>, starting with 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<you>' to watch, then move to p=quarantine and later p=reject.
